children.value: Find or build an image classification dataset, curate it, write a custom PyTorch
objects for it, then run inference with up to five pre-trained models from
. Compare the models using accuracy, precision, recall and F1-score, present the comparison with tables and visualizations, and close with a short analysis of why the models performed differently.
The dataset for this lab is

. It is a good fit for models pre-trained on ImageNet because ImageNet already contains both animals: classes 281–285 are domestic cats (tabby, tiger cat, Persian, Siamese, Egyptian cat) and classes 151–268 are 118 individual dog breeds. That means no training or fine-tuning is needed — each model predicts one of its 1,000 ImageNet classes, and that prediction is mapped back to
(anything that is neither, e.g. "lynx", "teddy bear", "wolf"). An
prediction always counts as a mistake, so the task is a little harder than a plain two-way choice.

(Vision Transformer). They were picked to cover different design ideas: a small and a large residual CNN, two lightweight mobile-oriented CNNs, and a transformer that has no convolutions after its first patch-embedding layer.

children.value: Raw scraped images are messy, so before anything touches a model each file goes through four checks:
— anything under 64 px on its shorter side would be upscaled almost 4× to reach 224 px, so it is dropped.
— the MD5 hash of the file bytes is used to remove exact copies.
, so grayscale or CMYK files do not break the 3-channel models.
are sampled with a fixed seed so the classes are perfectly balanced and the run is reproducible. They are copied into the standard one-folder-per-class layout,
file records each image's path and label.

CLASSES = ['cat', 'dog']
SRC_FOLDERS = {'cat': 'cats', 'dog': 'dogs'}
N_PER_CLASS = 500
MIN_SIDE = 64
DATA_DIR = os.path.join('data', 'lab7_cats_dogs')


def is_clean(path):
    try:
        with Image.open(path) as im:
            im.verify()
        with Image.open(path) as im:
            return min(im.size) >= MIN_SIDE
    except Exception:
        return False


def file_md5(path):
    with open(path, 'rb') as f:
        return hashlib.md5(f.read()).hexdigest()


rng = random.Random(42)
rows, log = [], []
for label, cls in enumerate(CLASSES):
    src = os.path.join(RAW_TEST, SRC_FOLDERS[cls])
    files = sorted(os.listdir(src))
    seen, clean = set(), []
    n_bad = n_dup = 0
    for fname in files:
        path = os.path.join(src, fname)
        if not is_clean(path):
            n_bad += 1
            continue
        digest = file_md5(path)
        if digest in seen:
            n_dup += 1
            continue
        seen.add(digest)
        clean.append(fname)

    chosen = sorted(rng.sample(clean, N_PER_CLASS))
    out_dir = os.path.join(DATA_DIR, cls)
    os.makedirs(out_dir, exist_ok=True)
    for fname in chosen:
        new_name = f"{cls}_{fname.split('.')[1]}.jpg"
        shutil.copy(os.path.join(src, fname), os.path.join(out_dir, new_name))
        rows.append({'filepath': f"{cls}/{new_name}", 'label': label, 'class_name': cls})
    log.append({'class': cls, 'raw files': len(files), 'unreadable / too small': n_bad,
                'duplicates': n_dup, 'clean': len(clean), 'sampled': len(chosen)})

labels_df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
labels_df.to_csv(os.path.join(DATA_DIR, 'labels.csv'), index=False)
pd.DataFrame(log)

A pre-trained model only works well if test images are prepared the same way as its training images. All five expect a 224×224 RGB tensor, but they differ in

they get there: the resize size before cropping (set by the crop percentage), the interpolation method, and the normalization statistics. The ViT checkpoint, for example, was trained with pixels scaled to [-1, 1] (mean 0.5, std 0.5) rather than the usual ImageNet mean/std. Feeding it the wrong normalization quietly costs accuracy. That is why each model gets its
pair built from its own transform.

children.value: Every model outputs 1,000 ImageNet logits per image.
takes the top-1 class and maps it: indices 281–285 →

switches off gradient tracking because nothing is being trained, which saves memory and time. The wall-clock time per image is also recorded (on this machine's CPU), since speed is part of what makes a model suitable or not.

CAT_IDX = range(281, 286)
DOG_IDX = range(151, 269)
IMAGENET_NAMES = models.ResNet18_Weights.IMAGENET1K_V1.meta['categories']
print('Cat classes :', [IMAGENET_NAMES[i] for i in CAT_IDX])
print('Dog classes :', len(DOG_IDX), 'breeds, e.g.', [IMAGENET_NAMES[i] for i in (151, 207, 235, 268)])


def imagenet_to_catdog(top1):
    out = torch.full_like(top1, 2)
    out[(top1 >= 281) & (top1 <= 285)] = 0
    out[(top1 >= 151) & (top1 <= 268)] = 1
    return out


@torch.no_grad()
def run_inference(model, loader):
    y_true, y_pred, top1_all, conf_all = [], [], [], []
    start = time.time()
    for xb, yb, _ in loader:
        probs = model(xb.to(device)).softmax(dim=1).cpu()
        conf, top1 = probs.max(dim=1)
        y_true.append(yb)
        y_pred.append(imagenet_to_catdog(top1))
        top1_all.append(top1)
        conf_all.append(conf)
    elapsed = time.time() - start
    return (torch.cat(y_true).numpy(), torch.cat(y_pred).numpy(),
            torch.cat(top1_all).numpy(), torch.cat(conf_all).numpy(), elapsed)


results = {}
for name, (model, _) in loaded.items():
    y_true, y_pred, top1, conf, elapsed = run_inference(model, loaders[name])
    results[name] = dict(y_true=y_true, y_pred=y_pred, top1=top1, conf=conf, seconds=elapsed)
    print(f"{name:16} done in {elapsed:6.1f} s  ({elapsed / len(y_true) * 1000:5.1f} ms / image)")

children.value: The four metrics answer slightly different questions:
— out of all 1,000 images, how many got the right animal?
— when the model says "cat", how often is it really a cat? (and the same for dog)
— out of all real cats, how many did the model find? (and the same for dog)
— the harmonic mean of precision and recall, high only if both are high.
), so cats and dogs count equally. An
prediction cannot raise precision for any class but it lowers recall, which is the right penalty for a model that looked at a cat and said "lynx". The "Other %" column shows how often that happened.

rows = []
for name, r in results.items():
    model = loaded[name][0]
    prec, rec, f1, _ = precision_recall_fscore_support(r['y_true'], r['y_pred'], labels=[0, 1],
                                                       average='macro', zero_division=0)
    rows.append({'Model': name,
                 'Accuracy': accuracy_score(r['y_true'], r['y_pred']),
                 'Precision': prec, 'Recall': rec, 'F1-score': f1,
                 'Other %': (r['y_pred'] == 2).mean() * 100,
                 'Params (M)': sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()) / 1e6,
                 'ms / image': r['seconds'] / len(r['y_true']) * 1000})

metrics_df = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index('Model').sort_values('F1-score', ascending=False)
metrics_df.style.format({'Accuracy': '{:.3f}', 'Precision': '{:.3f}', 'Recall': '{:.3f}', 'F1-score': '{:.3f}',
                         'Other %': '{:.1f}', 'Params (M)': '{:.1f}', 'ms / image': '{:.1f}'}) \
               .highlight_max(subset=['Accuracy', 'Precision', 'Recall', 'F1-score'], color='#cfe3f7')

Every model finds dogs much more easily than cats.

It has 118 dog classes but only 5 cat classes, so the models spent far more of their training on dog features and have far more "dog" outputs to land on. A blurry, dark, or partly hidden cat only has to look a little like one of 118 breeds to get pulled into the dog group. This is also why

Some mistakes come from the data, not the model.

779 of the 1,000 images were classified correctly by all five models, and only 17 fooled every one of them. The error gallery shows why most of those 17 are hard: several cats in one photo, a cat being held by people, a black cat in a dark room, a cat behind a cage, or a tiny cat in a low-resolution photo. One "cat" image is actually a grey

placeholder — a labelling error in the original Kaggle data that passed every automatic curation check (it opens fine, is big enough, and is not a duplicate). Only looking at the errors revealed it. A real project would remove it and do a manual review pass, but it is left in here so the reported numbers match what the pipeline actually produced.
Why the models differ — architecture and complexity.

splits the image into 196 patches of 16×16 pixels and uses self-attention, so every patch can look at every other patch from the very first layer. A CNN only sees a small neighbourhood per layer and builds up a global view slowly. Global context helps exactly in the hard cases above: a cat that fills only part of the frame, or is partly covered, can still be linked to its ears, eyes and tail elsewhere in the image. It is also the largest model (86.6 M parameters) and these weights were pre-trained on ImageNet-21k (about 14 million images) before being fine-tuned on ImageNet-1k, so it has seen far more animals than the CNNs. Transformers have weaker built-in assumptions about images than CNNs, and they need that much data to pay off.

is the cleanest comparison because both use the same design and the same training recipe; the only real difference is depth (50 vs. 18 layers) and bottleneck blocks. The deeper network gets +2.7 points of accuracy and fewer cat→dog mistakes (29 vs. 47), because it has more capacity to learn fine-grained features such as face shape and fur texture.

beats ResNet-18 with less than half the parameters (5.3 M vs. 11.7 M). Its depth, width and input resolution were balanced together (compound scaling), and its MBConv blocks use cheap depthwise convolutions plus squeeze-and-excitation, which lets the network re-weight channels based on what is in the whole image — a small step toward the global context that ViT has.

is the smallest (3.5 M) and fastest model. Its inverted-residual blocks are built for phones, trading some capacity for speed. It still matches ResNet-18 on accuracy, but it has the most cat→dog confusions (58), which suggests its smaller feature set does not separate the two animals as clearly.

All five take a 224×224 RGB image, but their preprocessing differs, and Section 6 printed each pipeline. The ResNets resize to 235 before cropping, the mobile models to 256, ViT to 248, and ViT normalizes with mean/std 0.5 instead of the usual ImageNet statistics. Giving each model its own transform is part of why the comparison is fair. Center-cropping also has a cost on this dataset: many photos are wide, and a cat sitting near the edge can be partly cut off before the model ever sees it. ViT is also locked to its 16-pixel patch grid and learned position embeddings, so running it at a different resolution would need those embeddings to be interpolated, while the CNNs would accept other sizes directly.

The accuracy-vs-speed plot shows a clear trade-off. ViT is about 7–10× slower per image than MobileNetV2 or EfficientNet-B0 on CPU for about 4–5 extra points of accuracy over MobileNetV2 (3.7 over EfficientNet-B0). ResNet-50 sits in the middle. For offline batch labelling of a photo collection, ViT-B/16 is the best choice. For a phone app or anything real-time,
is the sweet spot: almost ResNet-50 accuracy at ResNet-18 speed and a fifth of ResNet-50's size.

The more interesting finding is that every model shared the same weakness: cats were missed far more often than dogs, mostly being pulled toward the 118 dog classes or toward objects in the scene. That bias comes from the ImageNet label set, not from any one architecture, so picking a bigger model reduces the problem but does not remove it. The natural next step would be to fine-tune the final layer of each model on a two-class cat/dog head, which should close most of that gap, and to manually clean the remaining label noise such as the placeholder image found during error analysis.
